content: A speculum is a medical instrument designed for the examination of body cavities. Its shape and structure are specifically tailored to the cavity it is intended to investigate. Historically, the term diopter or dioptra was also used to refer to a speculum in older medical texts. Vaginal specula have been in use since ancient times, with evidence of their application by the Romans. Artifacts of vaginal specula have been discovered in Pompeii. The modern vaginal speculum, developed by J. Marion Sims, consists of a hollow cylindrical structure with a rounded end that is divided into two hinged parts, resembling the beak of a duck. This instrument is inserted into the vagina to dilate it, allowing for the examination of the vaginal walls and cervix. A specialized type of vaginal speculum, known as the weighted speculum, features a broad half-tube bent at approximately a 90-degree angle. The channel of the tube is positioned on the exterior side of the bend. One end of the tube is equipped with a roughly spherical metal weight that surrounds the channel. During vaginal surgery, the weighted speculum is placed in the vagina while the patient is in the lithotomy position. The weight stabilizes the speculum, freeing the surgeon's hands for other tasks. Vaginal specula are also utilized in anal surgery, although there are several other forms of anal specula available. One common type, the sigmoidoscope, is a tubular instrument with a removable bullet-shaped insert. When inserted into the rectum, the insert dilates the rectum to the diameter of the tube. The insert is then removed, leaving the tube in place to facilitate rectal examination. This design of anal speculum is one of the oldest surgical instrument designs still in use, with examples dating back centuries. Ear specula are funnel-shaped instruments available in various sizes, while nasal specula consist of two relatively flat blades with a handle. The nasal speculum is hinged, so squeezing the handles together causes the blades to spread laterally, allowing for examination of the nasal cavity. Traditionally, all specula were made of metal and sterilized after use. However, many modern specula, particularly those used in emergency departments and outpatient clinics, are now made of plastic. These plastic specula are sterile, disposable, and intended for single use. Specula used in surgical settings are still commonly made of metal. In addition to their medical applications, vaginal and anal specula are sometimes used as sexual devices. Contrary to some misconceptions, the use of a speculum does not cause damage to the vaginal opening, as attested by many gynecological experts. In the United States, the personal use of vaginal specula is illegal in a few states. However, due to the influence of the second-wave feminist movement, which promoted cervical self-examination, many states have relaxed or eliminated restrictions on speculum use. Despite this, distributors must adhere to specific guidelines regarding the sale of specula. For reference, the historical use of the term diopter can be found in the Compact Edition of the Oxford English Dictionary (Oxford University Press, 1971). Additionally, the historical context of specula is discussed in Cecilia Mettler's History of Medicine.
